AI large language models (LLMs) are disrupting all parts of our lives at breakneck
pace, and I am faced with the question:
**Could an AI decision model turn crop-disease observations and weather information into a defensible management recommendation?**  

As a scientist who specialises in pest and disease modelling, I am intrigued by
how AI decision models like [Jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev),
a class of AI model defined as “system one”, could be used for “decision support
tools” (DSTs).
The name, system one, draws on the distinction popularised in 
["Thinking Fast and Slow"](https://www.penguin.com.au/books/thinking-fast-and-slow-9780141033570). 
“System one” describes rapid, intuitive judgement, whereas “System two” describes 
slower, more deliberate reasoning, more akin to most LLMs. 
In this context, a system-one decision model is designed to map a stated 
situation directly to a choice, rather than generating a long chain of reasoning.  

## Why are AI decision models a big deal?  

Decision models like Jev are designed not to hallucinate.
They are written in TypeScript and described as “type-safe”.
They are bound by hard-coded rules, so they can't wander off into fanciful ideas.

![Hallucination and Type-safety, credit www.typesafe.ai](https://framerusercontent.com/images/KEoJ6ZaJkOZG6mcjBsOlB3NCqek.png?width=2048&height=633)  

<br>  

This makes them great candidates for decision tools because they can only
respond with specific options, for example: Yes or No, Left, right or straight. 
Or for a more abstract example, they respond like traffic lights. 
Defined conditions determine whether the signal is red, amber or green. 
The system doesn't suddenly invent a fourth colour because it thinks it might be 
useful.  

<br>  

> So are AI decision models useful for making management decisions in agriculture?  

The recent access to the [Jev playground](https://jevplayground.com/) allowed me
to evaluate this exact question.  

I decided to test Jev's ability by presenting the model with a scenario which 
could be faced by a vineyard manager observing downy mildew for the first time
in their vineyard. 
The grower must decide whether to apply a fungicide and, if so, when to spray
for maximum efficacy.


<br>

## Why downy mildew in grape vines?

In the 2023-24 growing season I undertook an experiment on downy mildew at a
vineyard on Mount Tamborine in Queensland, Australia.
With this work I was evaluating the performance of a mechanistic epidemiological
model which I translated from the academic literature into R as [`viticolR`](https://github.com/PaulMelloy/viticolR).
Dissecting this model gave me insight into the risk factors leading to problematic
downy mildew epidemics.  

<center>
![Students inspecting leaves for downy mildew](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PaulMelloy/downy_dst/main/viticolR_dst/www/InspectingLeaves.jpg){width=60%} 
</center>
<br>

## Downy mildew risk factors

Downy mildew (*Plasmopara viticola*) is an oomycete, which can overwinter in
leaf litter from infected plants of previous seasons.
The contaminated leaf litter contains oospores which, with suitable
temperature and moisture conditions, promote germination and macrosporangia
which, in turn, are triggered to release zoospores through rain splash.
Oospores and macrosporangia are the most likely source of primary infections in 
vineyards.  
<center>
![Downy mildew infection cycle Rossi et al (2008)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PaulMelloy/downy_dst/main/viticolR_dst/www/2008_Rossi_DownyPrimaryInfection.png)  
['A mechanistic model simulating primary infections of downy mildew in grapevine'](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304380007005881)
</center>

Once in the canopy, the disease can spread rapidly.
Infected leaves produce sporangia which spread more zoospores through rain splash
and sometimes wind and heavy dew.
Weather conditions that facilitate rapid disease cycles are typified by warm 
weather and rain.

<br>  

## Management strategies  

The ideal management strategy is to protect the crop with a fungicide spray ahead
of any potential dispersal events and prior to bunch closure. 
However, the value and permitted timing of another application depend on the product, 
crop stage, previous applications, resistance-management requirements and forecast 
conditions.
In general, synthetic fungicides such as strobilurins and DMIs are used early in
the season, with organically permissible fungicides like copper and bicarbonate applied
in between synthetic applications and later in the season.
This requires constant vigilance with an eye on weather forecasts and any potential
primary infections.

With this knowledge under our belt, let's see how Jev performs.

<br>  
<br>  

## Inputs always included
### **State**: context for the model  

> It is the 1st of November, a vineyard grower in Stanthorpe in Australia notices 
one plant in their vineyard shows signs of downy mildew. 
Downy mildew, caused by the oomycete Plasmopara viticola, is a major disease of 
grapevines that infects leaves, shoots, flowers and developing berries, 
particularly under warm, wet conditions. 
Infected leaves develop characteristic yellow “oil spots” that can progress to 
tissue death and premature leaf fall, while infection of flowers and young 
berries can cause browning, shrivelling and loss of fruit. 
Severe disease can substantially reduce grape yield and quality and, through 
extensive defoliation, reduce vine vigour and carbohydrate reserves needed for 
growth and production in subsequent seasons.

### Question  
> Which fungicide spray strategy should he undertake?  

### Decision type  
> Choice  

### Standard choices  

>  1. No fungicide spray  
  2. One fungicide spray today  
  3. One fungicide spray in 10 days  
  4. One fungicide spray in 20 days  
  5. One fungicide spray in 30 days  
  6. Two fungicide sprays: today and in 20 days  
  7. Two fungicide sprays: in 10 days and in 30 days  

<br>  

***  

## Scenario One  
### Additional input: **State**  

> The last fungicide application was metalaxyl 14 days ago.  
The remainder of the season is forecast to be wetter and warmer than average.  

### Output  

![](../../files/img/2610_JevScenario1.png){style="float: center" width=50%}  


### Interpretation  

The output assigns a relative score to each predefined option. 
Generally, the highest-scoring option indicates the preferred decision, but the
scores should not necessarily be treated as calibrated probabilities or as a
measure of agronomic correctness.

In this scenario, Jev’s preferred option broadly matches my assessment of the 
most defensible response.  

A fungicide spray at the earliest opportunity is the best option ahead of wet
conditions to limit the spread of the disease.
A follow-up spray in 20 days is also worth considering.

*I am suddenly a bit nervous ...*

<br>  

***  

## Scenario Two  
### Additional input: **State**  

> The last fungicide application was metalaxyl **7 days ago**.  
The remainder of the season is forecast to be drier and cooler than average.  

### Output  

![](../../files/img/2610_JevScenario2.png){style="float: center" width=50%}  

### Interpretation  

The model does not provide ideal recommendations here.  

The fungicide 7 days ago is still likely to be providing protection and with
cool dry conditions in the future, the grower is best off delaying their
fungicide spray.

*No longer questioning my career choices ...*

<br>  

***  

## Scenario Three  
### Additional input: **State**  

> The last fungicide application was metalaxyl **7 days ago**.  
There is no rain and dry conditions forecast over the next 30 days.  

### Output  

![](../../files/img/2610_JevScenario3.png){style="float: center" width=50%}  

### Interpretation  

Although confidence in “no fungicide” is increasing, immediate fungicide application
is still the highest-scoring response.

Despite downy mildew being present in the canopy, this is not a good recommendation.
The most risk-averse grower may consider a single application in 20–30
days, but not immediately.

*Hold my beer Jev!*  

<br>  

***  

## Scenario Four  
### Additional input: **State**  

> Edited: It is November 1st, a vineyard grower in Stanthorpe in Australia has no 
history of Downy Mildew and has not yet observed any Downy mildew in his vineyard.  
The last fungicide application was metalaxyl **7 days ago**.  
There is no rain and dry conditions forecast over the next 30 days.  

### Output  

![](../../files/img/2610_JevScenario4.png){style="float: center" width=50%}  

### Interpretation  

A good response. Finally, the decision model does not recommend a fungicide 
application. 
Under this deliberately low-risk scenario, Jev appropriately ranks 
“no fungicide spray” as the preferred option.

*There may be some hope for you yet Jev*  

***  

## Final thoughts  

Models like Jev are very new and the whole pace of change in AI development
is dizzyingly fast.
In this small test, Jev did not respond consistently enough to changing disease 
risk to be relied upon as a stand-alone agricultural decision-support system.
However, there is potential to use this approach in future research and development
frameworks.

I should also be fair and note that
[clear inputs and non-adversarial options are stated as highly important](https://jevplayground.com/what-is-jev#limits) 
for getting good answers with Jev. 
So perhaps my hastily prepared example here is too disingenuous for a real
world example, and the state input needs more specific guidance towards what
are important guardrails for making accurate decisions.
However, we frequently lack real world examples of the important thresholds
that guide our decision making, and decision models are no different.
Where models like this will provide specific benefits to agricultural decision
making is in their ability to consider a large number of dependent variables when
estimating the optimum choice.

> Regardless of how good AI models will get at providing advice, in the end
AI models are not accountable for the actions taken.

And for this reason humans will need to remain in the loop for all final decisions
no matter how intelligent the AI support will be.

While Jev remains closed source, some open-weight system one decision models such
as [Tev1](https://www.together.ai/models/tev1-4b-experimental) have been 
released publicly.
Who knows when we might be able to fine-tune these models to provide better
decision support for integrated pest management.
